title: Tortilla Chips 300g

drivers.name: Price increase to $3.97
drivers.evidence: Two prior weeks at $3.97 saw sales 106 and 75 (vs baseline 124.1), implying 15–40% decline; noise-adjusted effect ~x0.80. This price is 3.7% above regular.

drivers.name: Competitor store opening across the street
drivers.evidence: New competitive threat; no prior data, but plausible demand loss. Noted in planner notes. Affects local share; evidence is limited but plausible.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 124.1. A 3.7% price increase to $3.97 is likely to reduce demand, especially with a new competitor opening across the street. Past price hikes to $3.97 (2026-09-28, 2026-10-05) saw sales drop to 106 and 75 (vs baseline 124.1), implying a 20–39% decline. The competitor entry is a new, untested driver but plausible to reduce demand, especially given the price increase. No promotion or event is scheduled. The classical model suggests no uplift, but judgment overrides this. The combined effect is a downward shift. Evidence is moderate (2 past price spikes, 1 new competitor), so shrink toward 1.0. No seasonal or trend lift expected.

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 3.97 (+3.7% vs regular price 3.83)
  planner notes: A competitor opens a store across the street this week

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 124.1 | 5%-95%: 77.2 - 200.6 | 10%-90%: 88.7 - 170.3

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-29% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
